speaker: Michael Mauboussin
title: The Success Equation: Untangling Skill and Luck | Michael Mauboussin
question: In active institutional investing, why do fund returns look increasingly random and luck-driven?
guest: If I put investing on the luck-skill continuum, I would put it way over on the luck side, but it is not accurate to say that is because of a lack of skill. Most professional institutional investors are very skillful—they went to great schools and have incredible information access and computing power. The problem is that they are all doing the same thing, so their skill is extremely uniform. If I put you back in the 1960s with today's financial technology, you would run circles around everybody, but now everybody has the same thing, which leaves much more to luck. We measured the standard deviation of excess returns for money managers over the last 50 years, and that bell-shaped distribution has gotten skinnier. The difference between the very best and the average is less today than a generation or two ago. So outcomes are very random not because skill is absent, but because skill is very high and very uniform.

models.label: Claude Fable 5.2
models.answer:
The main explanation is what Michael Mauboussin calls the "paradox of skill": as investors become more skilled in absolute terms, the differences in skill between them shrink, so luck accounts for a larger share of the variation in results.

Active management is a relative game. Outperformance comes from exploiting other investors' mistakes, and those on the other side of trades are now mostly well-resourced professionals with similar training, data, models, and technology. Less-skilled participants (retail investors, weak managers) have largely migrated to index funds, removing the easy sources of alpha. With information disseminated near-instantly and regulations like Reg FD levelling access, prices incorporate news quickly and few edges persist.

When skill is uniformly high and tightly clustered, the dispersion of outcomes is dominated by noise: random factor exposures, timing, and style cycles. This shows up empirically as weak performance persistence: top-quartile funds rarely stay there (S&P's persistence scorecards), and after fees, most managers trail benchmarks. Studies such as Fama and French (2010) find the distribution of fund alphas is hard to distinguish from what chance alone would produce.

So managers haven't become worse; they've become uniformly good, making luck the deciding factor.

models.label: Gemini 4 Carbon
models.answer:
Active institutional returns look increasingly luck-driven not because managers have lost skill, but because absolute skill has risen and converged—a dynamic Michael Mauboussin calls the "paradox of skill." Today’s institutional investors draw from similar talent pools, quantitative models, alternative datasets, and computing power, while fair-disclosure rules have eliminated privileged corporate access. In any competition combining skill and chance, as participants become uniformly sophisticated, relative skill gaps shrink and randomness dominates outcomes.

Meanwhile, the migration toward passive index funds has removed many less-informed participants from active trading. Because alpha is zero-sum before fees, active managers now trade primarily against equally capable institutions rather than weaker counterparties. Faster price discovery quickly arbitrages away remaining mispricings, while institutional pressures—such as career risk, short evaluation horizons, and tight benchmark tracking—herd funds into crowded positions. With analytical and informational edges compressed and management fees deducting from gross returns, cross-sectional differences in fund performance increasingly reflect unpredictable market noise and luck rather than repeatable skill.

models.label: Claude Opus 5.5
models.answer:
This is what Michael Mauboussin calls the "paradox of skill." Active management has become intensely professionalized. Managers are well trained, have the same data, models and analytical tools, and react to news almost instantly. As skill rises across the industry, the *absolute* level of skill goes up, but the *variance* of skill between managers shrinks. When nearly everyone is very good, being skillful doesn't separate you from your competitors much.

Markets are competitive, so returns relative to a benchmark depend on how good you are compared with other participants, not on how good you are in absolute terms. Once skill differences narrow, random factors make up a larger share of the gap in outcomes. Those factors include unexpected news, timing, and which bets happened to pay off. Skill can't be diversified away like luck can, but it can be cancelled out when competitors are just as skilled.

The evidence fits this explanation. The spread of excess returns across funds has narrowed. Alpha persistence is weak. Studies such as Fama-French (2010) find that few managers outperform by more than chance would predict once fees are taken out. Luck therefore has an outsized effect on how results get ranked.

A strong track record can reflect skill, but returns alone often give you too little evidence to tell.
